title: Energy & Momentum Conservation
intro: Three big 'nothing is lost' rules explain a lot of the sky: momentum, angular momentum and energy are all conserved. Learn what each one is, the formulas (p = mv, L = mvr, E = ½ mv², E = mgh, E = mc²) and how to use them in collisions, orbits and spinning.

sections.title: What energy is

img.alt: Motion, height, heat, and light represent different forms of energy.

steps.title: Energy and work
bullets: **Energy** is the ability to do work or to make power. It can also show up as light or heat.
**Work** is force times distance. Pushing harder, or pushing over a longer distance, means more work.
Energy is measured in **joules (J)**: 1 J = 1 N × m = 1 kg × m²/s². The symbol for energy is E.

steps.title: Many forms, one idea
bullets: Forms of energy: work (mechanical), chemical, kinetic (motion), radiative (light), thermal (heat), potential (stored) and mass-energy (nuclear). The forms can overlap.
Energy can be changed from one form to another, but it can never be created or destroyed.

steps.title: How big is a joule?
bullets: A joule is small: sunlight delivers about 1.3 × 10³ J to each square metre every second, and a candy bar holds about 1 × 10⁶ J.
Food labels use Calories. **1 food Calorie is about 4184 J**, so the 2500 Calories an adult needs each day is about 10 million joules (1 × 10⁷ J).
Check: 2500 × 4184 = 10,460,000 J, which is close to 1 × 10⁷ J.

boxes.text: Why so many names? Energy hides in many places: a moving bike, a hot stove, a beam of light, a rock on a ledge. Giving each hiding place a name lets us follow where the energy goes.
Energy is like money you can swap between coins and bills. The form changes, but the total stays the same.

Unit mix-up: the joule (J) is energy, the newton (N) is force, and kg × m/s is momentum. Slide 1 gives 1 J = 1 N × m = 1 kg × m²/s². The textbook adds that 1 food Calorie is about 4184 J (not on the slides).

Textbook inconsistency: Table 4.1 gives 3.4 × 10⁷ J for burning 1 liter of oil, but Mathematical Insight 4.2 uses 12 million J (1.2 × 10⁷ J). Use the number the question gives. Both values are far below 9 × 10¹⁶ J, so the conclusion of the rock example does not change.

sourceNotes: Cosmic Perspective 4.3, 'Basic Types of Energy' and Table 4.1 (p.120)

sections.title: Three basic kinds of energy

img.alt: Three photos joined by arrows: racing cyclists for kinetic energy, sunlight on a sunflower for radiative energy and a gasoline pump for potential energy.

steps.title: Motion, light, stored
bullets: Nearly all energy fits **three groups**: kinetic (energy of motion, like the racing cyclists), radiative (energy carried by light, like sunlight) and potential (stored energy, like the gasoline).
The arrows show that energy can change from any group into another, but it is never created or destroyed.
Light carries energy, which is why it can warm the surface of a planet or change molecules in our eyes so we can see.

steps.title: Where each form fits
bullets: **Thermal energy** (heat) is kinetic energy: it is the total motion energy of many jiggling particles.
Gravitational potential energy, chemical energy (food, gasoline) and mass-energy are all stored energy, so they are kinds of potential energy.
Falling rocks, orbiting planets and moving air molecules all have kinetic energy.

boxes.text: Why only three groups? Whatever energy is doing, it is either moving things, riding on light, or waiting to be released. Every other name is a special case of one of these.
Move, Light, Store: kinetic, radiative, potential.

The slides list seven forms and say they overlap. The textbook sorts nearly all energy into three groups: kinetic (motion), radiative (light) and potential (stored). Thermal counts as a kind of kinetic energy and mass-energy as a kind of potential energy. Know the slide list and where each form fits.

sourceNotes: Cosmic Perspective 4.3, 'Basic Types of Energy' and Figure 4.11 (p.120)

sections.title: Kinetic energy: the energy of motion

img.alt: A cyclist riding fast with a blurred background, above the kinetic energy formula in a red box.

steps.title: Moving things carry energy
bullets: **Kinetic energy** is the energy of a moving object. It grows with mass and grows even faster with speed.
Formula: **E = ½ × m × v²** (m = mass in kg, v = speed in m/s, E in joules).
Example: a 2 kg ball at 3 m/s has E = ½ × 2 × 3 × 3 = 9 J.

steps.title: Doubling speed quadruples energy
bullets: Speed is squared, so double the speed and the energy is **4 times** bigger. Triple it and the energy is 9 times bigger. Double the mass at the same speed and the energy only doubles.
A 70 kg cyclist at 10 m/s has ½ × 70 × 10² = 3500 J. At 5 m/s the same cyclist has 875 J, exactly 4 times less.
A 1000 kg car at 20 m/s has ½ × 1000 × 20² = 200,000 J. At 30 m/s (1.5 times faster) it has 450,000 J, which is 1.5² = 2.25 times more.

steps.title: Same energy, different momentum
bullets: A 4000 kg truck at 10 m/s has ½ × 4000 × 10² = 200,000 J. A 1000 kg car at 20 m/s has ½ × 1000 × 20² = 200,000 J. The kinetic energies are equal.
Their momenta are not: the truck has 4000 × 10 = 40,000 kg × m/s and the car has 1000 × 20 = 20,000 kg × m/s.
Energy counts speed twice (v²) and momentum counts it once (v), so the two measures can rank objects differently.

boxes.text: Why does speed matter more than mass? Speed is multiplied by itself (v × v), but mass only counts once. A small fast object can carry more energy than a big slow one.
Mass counts once, speed counts twice.
Slide 3 writes 'velocity', the textbook writes 'speed' in E = ½ mv². Either way the answer is the same because v is squared. Do not use E = mv (that is momentum, not energy) and do not forget the ½.

sourceNotes: Practice questions Q16 (car speed doubles); the cyclist, car and truck numbers are worked examples made for this site (outside source)

images.alt: A cyclist riding fast with a blurred background, above the kinetic energy formula in a red box.

img.alt: Two cubes of particles with arrows; the right cube has longer arrows, so its particles move faster.

steps.title: Jiggling particles
bullets: **Thermal energy** is the collective kinetic energy of all the particles (atoms and molecules) in a substance.
In the picture the right cube has longer arrows, so its particles move faster and it is hotter.
Even a still object has thermal energy, because its particles never stop jiggling.

img.alt: Three thermometers (Kelvin, Celsius, Fahrenheit) marking where water boils, where water freezes and absolute zero.

steps.title: Temperature scales
bullets: **Temperature** is the average kinetic energy of the particles in a substance.
Water boils at 373.15 K = 100 °C = 212 °F, and freezes at 273.15 K = 0 °C = 32 °F.
**Absolute zero** is 0 K = -273.15 °C = -459.67 °F, the coldest possible. The Kelvin scale never goes negative.

img.alt: A pot of boiling water at 212 °F beside an oven at 400 °F, with many more particles drawn in the pot than in the oven.

steps.title: Hot oven versus boiling pot
bullets: Thermal energy is the **total** kinetic energy, so it depends on both the temperature AND the amount of matter.
Oven air (about 400 °F = 200 °C) is hotter than boiling water (212 °F = 100 °C), but the pot holds more thermal energy because water is much denser, so there are far more particles.
That is why boiling water scalds a hand at once, while a quick dip in oven air is much less harmful.

boxes.text: Why does a pot of water burn you faster than oven air that is hotter? Energy reaches your skin when particles hit it. Water packs many more particles into the same space, so many more hits happen each second, even though each hit is a little weaker.
Temperature = average per particle. Thermal energy = total for all the particles. Think of a crowd: average running speed versus the whole crowd's running.

Hotter does not always mean more thermal energy. Practice question 18: a large pot of boiling water (100 °C) has more thermal energy than a tiny firework spark (1000 °C), because the pot has vastly more particles. Also, slide 5 shows no negative Kelvin values, so 'Kelvin can be negative' is the false statement.

sections.title: Gravitational potential energy

steps.title: Height stores energy
bullets: **Gravitational potential energy** is energy stored in an object because of its height. Nothing about the object has changed, but it can fall.
Formula: **E = m × g × h** (g = acceleration of gravity, about 10 m/s² on Earth, more exactly 9.8 m/s²; h = height).
Example: a 5 kg rock held 10 m up (g = 10 m/s²) stores 5 × 10 × 10 = 500 J.

img.alt: A ball thrown in an arc from a hand: more potential energy and less kinetic energy at the top, less potential and more kinetic energy near the ground.

steps.title: Trading height for speed
bullets: In the picture the total energy (kinetic + potential) is the same at every point of the flight.
Going up, kinetic energy turns into potential energy. Coming down, potential energy turns back into kinetic energy, so the ball is fastest near the ground.
Example: a 2 kg ball dropped from 5 m (g = 10 m/s², no air) has 100 J of potential energy. Just before landing that is 100 J of kinetic energy, so ½ × 2 × v² = 100 and v = 10 m/s.

img.alt: A big gray gas cloud with more stored gravitational energy shrinking into a small hot glow with less stored energy and more thermal energy.

steps.title: Stars heat up the same way
bullets: A cloud of gas shrinking under its own gravity loses gravitational potential energy: the big cloud has more stored energy, the small glow has less.
That lost potential energy becomes thermal energy and radiation, which makes the center of the cloud hot.

boxes.text: Why is a ball fastest at the bottom? At the top all its energy is stored (potential). As it falls, the stored energy changes into motion energy. The most motion energy, and so the highest speed, comes when the stored energy is lowest, near the ground.
Higher means more stored. Falling means stored turns into motion, like letting go of a squeezed spring.

The slide gives E = mgh without a value for g. The textbook says g = 9.8 m/s², or about 10 m/s². Use the value the question gives. The star-heating idea is only in the textbook (4.3, Figure 4.15b), not on the slides.

sourceNotes: Cosmic Perspective 4.3, 'Potential Energy in Astronomy' and Figure 4.15 (p. 121-122)

images.alt: A ball thrown in an arc from a hand: more potential energy and less kinetic energy at the top, less potential and more kinetic energy near the ground.
A big gray gas cloud with more stored gravitational energy shrinking into a small hot glow with less stored energy and more thermal energy.

sections.title: Mass-energy: E = mc²

img.alt: A glowing mushroom cloud from a nuclear explosion.

steps.title: Mass is stored energy
bullets: **Mass** is itself a form of energy: **E = mc²** (m = mass, c = speed of light, about 3 × 10⁸ m/s).
Inside stars, **nuclear fusion** turns a small amount of mass into energy, following Einstein's relation.
A small amount of mass becomes an enormous amount of energy. For 1 kg fully converted: E = 1 × (3 × 10⁸)² = 9 × 10¹⁶ J.

steps.title: Worked example: a 1 kg rock
bullets: E = mc² = 1 kg × (3 × 10⁸ m/s)² = 9 × 10¹⁶ J.

Burning 1 liter of oil gives about 1.2 × 10⁷ J, so the rock holds 9 × 10¹⁶ / 1.2 × 10⁷ = 7.5 × 10⁹ times more. That is about 7.5 billion liters of oil, roughly what all cars in the United States burn in a week.
A 1-megaton H-bomb converts only about 0.1 kg of mass into energy. The relation also works backward: energy can turn into mass, as in the early universe and in particle accelerators.

boxes.text: Why is the energy so huge? The speed of light is enormous, and it is squared. So c² is about 9 × 10¹⁶ and multiplies the mass. Even a pinch of mass is a mountain of energy.
c² is a gigantic multiplier: tiny mass in, giant energy out.

The slides use the letter E for kinetic energy (½ mv²) and for mass-energy (mc²), so read which formula the question needs. The value c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s and the 9 × 10¹⁶ J for 1 kg come from the textbook (Mathematical Insight 4.2), not the slides. The textbook also says a 1-megaton H-bomb converts only about 0.1 kg of mass.

sourceNotes: Cosmic Perspective 4.3, 'Potential Energy in Astronomy' and Mathematical Insight 4.2 (p. 122)

sections.title: Conservation of energy

img.alt: A ball exchanges gravitational potential, kinetic, and thermal energy while the total remains conserved.

steps.title: Energy is never created or destroyed
bullets: **Conservation of energy**: energy can only be changed from one form to another, never created or destroyed.
An object gains or loses energy only by trading it with other objects.
Kinetic, thermal and gravitational potential energy are the three forms to know.

steps.title: Where does lost energy go?
bullets: When something slows down by friction or air drag, its kinetic energy turns into thermal energy in the air or ground.
That heat can be hard to trace, but the energy never disappears.

steps.title: Tracing energy back
bullets: A thrown baseball gets its motion energy from the arm, the arm from chemical energy in the muscles, the muscles from food, and the food from sunlight.
The sunlight came from nuclear fusion, which releases mass-energy stored in the Sun's hydrogen, and that hydrogen came from the Big Bang.
After the throw, the ball's kinetic energy ends up as thermal energy in the air or ground. It may be hard to trace, but it never disappears.

boxes.text: Why can no machine give free energy? Because energy cannot appear from nothing. Any energy a machine delivers must have come from somewhere else, such as fuel, light, height or mass.
Energy only changes costumes: motion, heat, light, stored. The actor underneath stays the same.

Wrong-answer pattern: 'the explosion creates new energy' (practice Q14 option A) or 'energy is used up' are always false. A satellite that drops because of air drag loses orbital energy, but that energy turns into heat (practice Q19), so the total is still conserved. The orbit idea comes from later material; the 'never disappears' idea is in the textbook (4.3).

sourceNotes: Cosmic Perspective 4.3, 'Where do objects get their energy?' (p. 120)

sections.title: Conservation of momentum

img.alt: A pool table with many colored balls and a cue.

steps.title: Momentum = mass × velocity
bullets: **Momentum** is mass times velocity: p = m × v, in kg × m/s. It has a direction, so it can be positive or negative.
In a closed system the **total momentum is conserved**: pool balls have the same total momentum before and after they collide.
Example: a 1000 kg car at 20 m/s has p = 1000 × 20 = 20,000 kg × m/s.

img.alt: A moving white ball hits a still yellow ball; before the hit the white ball has all the momentum, after the hit the yellow ball does.

steps.title: Before and after a collision
bullets: **Conservation of momentum**: the total momentum of a set of objects cannot change unless an outside force acts on them.
In the picture a moving ball hits a still ball. Before: first ball has m × v, second has 0. After: first has 0, second has m × v. The total is the same.

img.alt: A small spacecraft coasting in the dark of space, with the note that a spaceship needs no fuel to keep moving.

steps.title: Why objects keep moving
bullets: With no outside force, momentum cannot change, so an object keeps the same velocity. A spacecraft that shuts its engines in deep space coasts in a straight line at constant speed.
Interacting objects swap momentum through equal and opposite forces.

img.alt: A rocket lifting off on a trail of exhaust gas.

steps.title: Rockets and rifles recoil
bullets: The total momentum of a rocket and its gas stays zero, so the forward momentum of the rocket equals the backward momentum of the gas it shoots out.
Rocket: a 500 kg rocket expels 5 kg of gas backward at 1000 m/s. The gas has 5 × 1000 = 5000 kg × m/s backward, so 500 × v = 5000 and the rocket gains v = 10 m/s forward.
Rifle: a 4 kg rifle fires a 0.01 kg bullet at 400 m/s. The bullet has 4 kg × m/s forward, so the rifle recoils with 4 × v = 4, which is 1 m/s backward.

steps.title: Jumping pushes Earth too
bullets: When you jump, your legs push Earth the other way and give it an equal and opposite kick of momentum.
Earth's huge mass makes its change in speed too small to notice. Gravity later pulls you back down and returns the momentum, so the total never changes.

boxes.text: Why does a spaceship need no fuel to keep coasting? In empty space nothing pushes on it, so its momentum cannot change. It keeps the same speed and direction.
Momentum is passed, never made: like a ball passed in basketball, the team's total stays the same.

Momentum (m × v) is not kinetic energy (½ m v²). Momentum has direction and can be negative; energy cannot. Practice Q13: a spacecraft that shuts its engines in deep space keeps moving in a straight line at constant speed. Practice Q14: a rifle kicks back because the bullet's forward momentum is matched by the rifle's backward momentum, not because energy is created.

sourceNotes: Cosmic Perspective 4.3, 'Why do objects move at constant velocity...' (p.118, Figure 4.8) and 4.2 (Figure 4.6, rocket and spaceship)
Practice questions Q13 and Q14; the rocket and rifle numbers are worked examples made for this site (outside source)

sections.title: Pool-ball collision puzzles

img.alt: A red ball moving right with speed lines toward a black 8-ball at rest, labeled red: 2 m/s right and black: at rest.

steps.title: Red hits black
bullets: A red ball moves right at 2 m/s and hits an identical black ball at rest. Before: total momentum = m × 2 (right) and kinetic energy = ½ m × 2² = 2m.
Test any collision story with two checks: (1) total momentum before and after must match, watching signs (right is positive, left is negative); (2) total kinetic energy can never go up.

img.alt: The red ball stopped and the black 8-ball moving right at 2 m/s.

steps.title: Red stops, black moves on: YES
bullets: If the red ball stops and the black ball moves right at 2 m/s, the total momentum is m × 2 before and m × 2 after. Energy is also the same (½ m × 2 × 2 both times). So it is **possible**.

img.alt: The red ball moving left at 2 m/s and the black 8-ball staying at rest.

steps.title: Red bounces back, black stays: NO
bullets: After this collision the red ball has momentum -2m (moving left) and the black ball has 0, so the total is -2m.
Before, the total was +2m. The total changed with no outside force, so **momentum is not conserved** and this is impossible.

img.alt: The red ball moving left at 2 m/s and the black 8-ball moving right at 4 m/s.

steps.title: Red bounces back, black at 4 m/s: NO
bullets: Momentum check: -2m + 4m = 2m. That matches the +2m before, so momentum is fine.
Energy check: before = ½ m × 2 × 2 = 2m. After = 2m (red) + ½ m × 4 × 4 = 8m (black), total 10m. The energy would jump from 2m to 10m, so **energy is not conserved** and it is impossible.

steps.title: Energy can drop, never rise
bullets: Take a 0.2 kg red ball at 2 m/s hitting an identical black ball at rest. If the red ball keeps going at 0.5 m/s, momentum gives 0.2 × 2 = 0.2 × 0.5 + 0.2 × v, so the black ball moves at v = 1.5 m/s.
The 0.15 J that went missing became heat and sound, so total energy is still conserved. Kinetic energy may fall but cannot rise.

boxes.text: Why do we test both laws? A collision must keep the total momentum the same AND must not create energy. Some wrong stories pass one test and fail the other, so check both.
Two checks, in order: P (momentum, watch the signs) then E (energy, never goes up from nothing).

Slide 9 says 'energy not conserved' for case (c). That works if the balls have equal mass, which the slide does not state but the picture suggests. Practice Test 2 Q11 (curling stones) is the same idea as case (b): the answer is 'violates conservation of momentum'. In that scenario the kinetic energy is actually unchanged (½ mv² before and after), so choosing 'violates energy conservation' is the trap. In real collisions some kinetic energy is often lost as heat and sound (outside source); the exam only asks about gaining energy or changing total momentum.

sections.title: Angular momentum and torque

img.alt: An oval orbit around a yellow Sun with arrows for speed v and dotted lines for distance r at the closest and farthest points.

steps.title: Moving on a curve
bullets: Objects moving on curved paths or spinning have **angular momentum**.
Formula: **L = m × v × r**, where v is the speed perpendicular to the radius and r is the distance from the center.
In the picture the planet is close to the Sun with a short r and a long speed arrow at the bottom, and far from the Sun with a long r and a short speed arrow at the top.

img.alt: Earth circling the Sun, with labels for its rotational angular momentum from spinning and its orbital angular momentum from going around the Sun.

steps.title: Spin and orbit
bullets: Earth has two kinds of angular momentum: **rotational** (from spinning once a day) and **orbital** (from circling the Sun).
Only a **torque**, a twisting force, can change angular momentum. A push on a door's hinges does nothing, but a light push at the far edge swings it.
That is why a longer wrench turns a bolt more easily: pushing from farther out gives more torque.

img.alt: An oval orbit around the Sun: where the distance r is greater the velocity v is smaller, and where r is smaller v is greater.

steps.title: No twist, no change
bullets: Earth feels no torque as it orbits the Sun, so its angular momentum stays the same and its orbit continues without any push or fuel.
Because L = m × v × r stays constant, Earth moves faster when closer to the Sun and slower when farther away.
Example: Earth is about 147 million km from the Sun in January (speed about 30.3 km/s) and 152 million km in July, so v = 30.3 × 147 / 152 ≈ 29.3 km/s.

boxes.text: Why is it called a twisting force? Try opening a door: pushing on the hinges does nothing, but a light push at the far edge swings it. Torque depends on how hard you push and where you push.
r and v trade places: when one goes up the other goes down, so m × v × r stays put.

Slide 11 says Earth's orbit 'will continue indefinitely'. The textbook adds that Earth slowly passes some of its spin angular momentum to the Moon, so Earth's rotation is gradually slowing (4.3 and 4.5). Orbit and spin are different angular momenta. Also: a torque changes angular momentum, an ordinary net force changes ordinary momentum. The faster-near-the-Sun result comes from the textbook (Figure 4.9) and is Kepler's second law.

sourceNotes: Cosmic Perspective 4.3, 'What keeps a planet rotating and orbiting the Sun?' (p. 118-119, Figure 4.9) and 4.1 (torque, door example)
Earth January and July distances and the 30.3 km/s speed are standard values (outside source)

sections.title: Spinning faster when radius shrinks

img.slide: textbook p.119 / Figure 4.10 (slide 12 shows the same idea)
img.alt: A skater spinning with arms stretched out, then spinning faster with arms pulled in, with labels for radius and speed of rotation.

steps.title: The skater pulls in his arms
bullets: With arms out the radius is large and the spin is slow. Pulling the arms in makes the radius small and the spin **faster**.
Angular momentum L = m × v × r stays the same, so a smaller r means a bigger v.
Example: a 2 kg ball whirled at 3 m/s on a 4 m string has L = 24 kg × m²/s. Shorten the string to 2 m and the speed becomes 6 m/s.

steps.title: Same rule in space and with ropes
bullets: A cowboy letting out more rope makes the radius bigger, so the loop goes around more slowly.
A big spinning star that collapses into a tiny neutron star spins much faster, because its radius shrank while its angular momentum stayed the same.
Gas clouds in space spin faster as gravity shrinks them, which helps explain why galaxies and young star systems form spinning disks.

boxes.text: Why must the speed go up when the radius goes down? The product m × v × r cannot change with no torque. If the mass stays the same and r is cut in half, v must double to keep the product the same.
Tuck in to spin fast, stretch out to slow down.

A faster spin does NOT mean more angular momentum. L is the same before and after; only r and v trade. Practice Q15: wrong options say L increases (C) or decreases (D) or the star spins slower. Practice Test 2 Q12 (lasso): longer rope, bigger r, slower rotation. Also, it is the product that is constant, not v or r alone.

bullets: Each law has the same pattern: a total stays fixed unless something from outside changes it.

Mass times velocity: p = m × v.
The total momentum of a set of objects cannot change unless an external force acts on them.
cards.short: Total momentum fixed without outside force

cards.front: Why interacting objects trade momentum evenly
cards.back: They exchange momentum through equal and opposite forces.
cards.short: Equal and opposite forces swap momentum

cards.front: Red ball (2 m/s) stops and black ball (at rest) moves at 2 m/s
cards.back: Possible. Momentum and energy are both the same before and after.
cards.short: Possible: red stops, black takes 2 m/s

cards.front: Red ball bounces back at 2 m/s and black ball stays still
cards.back: Impossible. Momentum is not conserved (+2m before, -2m after).

cards.front: Red ball bounces back at 2 m/s and black ball moves right at 4 m/s
cards.back: Impossible. Momentum balances, but the kinetic energy would rise from 2m to 10m, so energy is not conserved.
The momentum of objects on curved paths or spinning. L = mass × radius × velocity perpendicular to the radius.
cards.short: Momentum of spinning or curving objects

cards.back: L = m × v(perpendicular) × r.
An external twisting force. Angular momentum cannot change unless a torque acts.
The angular momentum of an object cannot change unless an external torque is applied.

cards.front: Why Earth's orbit needs no push
cards.back: Earth feels no torque in orbit, so its angular momentum stays the same and the orbit continues.
cards.src: Momentum deck slide 11; slide 9 of energy deck

cards.front: Why a skater spins faster pulling in her arms
cards.back: Angular momentum is conserved, so a smaller radius means a faster rotation speed.

cards.front: Why Earth moves faster nearer the Sun
cards.back: L = mvr is constant, so when r is smaller, v must be larger (and slower when farther away).

cards.front: Why objects keep constant velocity when no force acts
cards.back: Because of conservation of momentum: without an external force the momentum cannot change.

cards.front: The three basic categories of energy
cards.back: Kinetic (motion), radiative (light) and potential (stored). Thermal, chemical, gravitational and mass-energy are subtypes.
Energy carried by light. It can warm a planet's surface or change molecules in our eyes.
1 food Calorie is about 4184 J, so 2500 Calories a day is about 10 million joules.

cards.front: Recoil rule from conservation of momentum
cards.back: When something starts at rest and splits, m1 × v1 = m2 × v2 in opposite directions (bullet and rifle, gas and rocket).

quiz.q: A 1500 kg car travelling at 20 m/s brakes to a complete stop. By conservation of energy, about how much kinetic energy is converted into thermal energy in the brakes, tires and road?
quiz.why: Kinetic energy = ½ × 1500 × 20² = ½ × 1500 × 400 = 300,000 J, and all of it becomes thermal energy. Using mv gives 30,000 and dropping the ½ gives 600,000.
quiz.source: Energy deck slides 3, 9 (numbers made for this site, outside source)

quiz.q: If a car's speed doubles, its kinetic energy
options: stays the same.
doubles.
triples.
increases by a factor of 4.
is cut in half.
quiz.why: Speed is squared in E = ½ mv², so doubling v gives 2 × 2 = 4 times the energy.
quiz.source: Energy deck slide 3; Practice questions Q16

quiz.q: A 4000 kg truck travels at 10 m/s and a 1000 kg car travels at 20 m/s along the same road. Which statement is correct?
options: The truck has more kinetic energy and more momentum.
The car has more kinetic energy, and the truck has more momentum.
They have equal kinetic energy, and the truck has more momentum.
They have equal kinetic energy and equal momentum.
The car has more kinetic energy and more momentum.
quiz.why: Kinetic energy: truck ½ × 4000 × 10² = 200,000 J and car ½ × 1000 × 20² = 200,000 J, so they are equal. Momentum: truck 4000 × 10 = 40,000 and car 1000 × 20 = 20,000 kg × m/s, so the truck has more.
quiz.source: Energy deck slide 3; Momentum deck slide 3 (numbers made for this site, outside source)

quiz.q: In deep space, a rocket starts at rest. The rocket body (without the gas) has mass 500 kg. It expels 5 kg of hot gas backward at 1000 m/s. What is the rocket's speed forward afterwards?
options: 5 m/s
20 m/s
10 m/s
quiz.why: The gas has 5 × 1000 = 5000 kg × m/s of momentum backward. Total momentum started at zero, so the rocket gets 5000 kg × m/s forward: 500 × v = 5000, so v = 10 m/s.
quiz.source: Momentum deck slide 2; Cosmic Perspective 4.3 (rocket and conservation of momentum) and 4.2 Figure 4.6 (numbers made for this site, outside source)

quiz.q: A 0.5 kg ball is thrown straight up at 10 m/s from the ground. Ignoring air and using g = 10 m/s², how high does it rise?
options: 5 m
quiz.why: Starting kinetic energy ½ × 0.5 × 10² = 25 J becomes potential energy at the top: 0.5 × 10 × h = 25, so h = 5 m. The mass cancels: h = v²/(2g) = 100/20 = 5 m.
quiz.source: Energy deck slides 3 and 8; Cosmic Perspective Figure 4.15a (numbers made for this site, outside source)

img.alt: A ball thrown in an arc from a hand, with more potential energy at the top and more kinetic energy near the ground.

quiz.q: A 2 kg ball is dropped from a height of 5 m. Ignore air and use g = 10 m/s². How fast is it moving just before it lands?
options: 5 m/s
20 m/s
10 m/s
50 m/s
quiz.why: Potential energy at the top is 2 × 10 × 5 = 100 J. By conservation of energy all of it becomes kinetic energy, so ½ × 2 × v² = 100, v² = 100 and v = 10 m/s.
quiz.source: Energy deck slides 3 and 8

quiz.q: Use c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s. A 1 kg rock is completely converted into energy. Burning 1 liter of oil releases about 1.2 × 10⁷ J. About how many times more energy does the rock release?
options: 7.5 × 10⁶ times
2.5 × 10⁹ times
1.3 × 10⁻¹⁰ times
7.5 × 10⁹ times
7.5 × 10⁸ times
quiz.why: E = mc² = 1 × (3 × 10⁸)² = 9 × 10¹⁶ J. Dividing: 9 × 10¹⁶ / 1.2 × 10⁷ = 7.5 × 10⁹. Forgetting to square c, or flipping the ratio, gives the wrong powers of ten.
quiz.source: Cosmic Perspective Mathematical Insight 4.2 (p.122); Energy deck slide 7

quiz.q: A 2 kg ball is whirled in a circle at 3 m/s on a 4 m string (velocity perpendicular to the string). The string is then pulled in to 2 m with no outside torque. What are the new speed and the angular momentum?
options: 3 m/s and 12 kg × m²/s
6 m/s and 24 kg × m²/s
6 m/s and 12 kg × m²/s
12 m/s and 48 kg × m²/s
1.5 m/s and 24 kg × m²/s
quiz.why: L = m v r = 2 × 3 × 4 = 24 kg × m²/s and it stays 24. With r = 2 m: 2 × v × 2 = 24, so v = 6 m/s. Half the radius means double the speed, and L does not change.
quiz.source: Momentum deck slides 10-12 (numbers made for this site, outside source)

quiz.q: Earth is about 147 million km from the Sun in early January and about 152 million km in early July. Its orbital speed in January is about 30.3 km/s. Use conservation of angular momentum to estimate its speed in July.
quiz.why: m × v × r is constant, so v(July) = 30.3 × 147 / 152 = 4454 / 152 ≈ 29.3 km/s. Farther from the Sun means slower. Flipping the ratio gives 31.3, which is the wrong direction.
quiz.source: Cosmic Perspective 4.3, Figure 4.9 (distances and January speed are standard values, outside source); Momentum deck slides 10-11

img.alt: An oval orbit around the Sun: where the distance r is greater the velocity v is smaller, and where r is smaller v is greater.

quiz.q:
Which statements about angular momentum are correct?
I. Earth moves faster in its orbit when it is closer to the Sun.
II. A planet needs a continuing twisting push (torque) to keep orbiting the Sun.
III. A skater who pulls in her arms spins faster.
options: I only
II only
I and III only
II and III only
all of the above
quiz.why: I is true because m × v × r is constant, so a smaller r means a larger v. II is false: with no torque the angular momentum stays the same and the orbit continues by itself. III is true for the same reason.
quiz.source: Momentum deck slides 10-12; Cosmic Perspective 4.3, Figures 4.9 and 4.10

quiz.q: A 4 kg rifle, initially at rest, fires a 0.01 kg bullet at 400 m/s. Which pair of statements is correct?
options: The rifle recoils backward at 1 m/s, and the bullet ends up with 400 times more kinetic energy than the rifle.
The rifle recoils backward at 1 m/s, and the bullet and the rifle end up with equal kinetic energy.
The rifle recoils backward at 1 m/s, and the rifle ends up with more kinetic energy than the bullet.
The rifle recoils backward at 100 m/s, and the bullet ends up with more kinetic energy than the rifle.
The rifle recoils backward at 4 m/s, and since the momenta are equal the kinetic energies are equal.
quiz.why: Bullet momentum = 0.01 × 400 = 4 kg × m/s forward, so the rifle gets 4 kg × m/s backward: 4 × v = 4, v = 1 m/s. Kinetic energies: bullet ½ × 0.01 × 400² = 800 J and rifle ½ × 4 × 1² = 2 J, a ratio of 400. Equal momentum does not mean equal energy.
quiz.source: Momentum deck slides 2-3; Practice questions Q14 (numbers made for this site, outside source)

quiz.q:
A red ball moving right at 2 m/s hits an identical black ball at rest. Which outcomes are possible?
I. The red ball stops and the black ball moves right at 2 m/s.
II. The red ball bounces back at 2 m/s and the black ball stays still.
III. The red ball bounces back at 2 m/s and the black ball moves right at 4 m/s.
options: I only
II only
I and III only
II and III only
all of the above
quiz.why: I keeps both momentum and energy. II changes the total momentum from +2m to -2m. III keeps momentum (-2m + 4m = +2m) but raises the energy from 2m to 10m.
quiz.source: Momentum deck slides 4-9

img.alt: A red ball moving right toward a black 8-ball at rest, labeled red: 2 m/s right and black: at rest.

quiz.q: Suppose a curling stone is slid towards another identical stone that is stationary. Which of the following correctly describes a scenario where, after colliding, the first stone travels back at the same speed while the second stone remains stationary?
options: Such a scenario is impossible, as it violates Newton's third law.
Such a scenario can happen in reality, as momentum and energy are both conserved.
Such a scenario is impossible, as it violates energy conservation.
Such a scenario is impossible, as it violates conservation of momentum.
Such a scenario is impossible, as it violates mass-energy equivalence.
quiz.why: Momentum before is +mv and after is -mv, so it changes with no outside force. The kinetic energy is actually unchanged (½ mv² both times), so energy is not the problem.
quiz.source: Practice Test 2 Q11; Momentum deck slides 6-7

quiz.q: A 0.2 kg red ball moving right at 2 m/s hits an identical black ball at rest. Afterwards the red ball moves left at 2 m/s and the black ball moves right at 4 m/s. Which statement is correct?
options: Momentum is violated, and the total kinetic energy afterwards is 0.8 J.
Energy is violated: the total kinetic energy afterwards is 2.0 J, up from 0.4 J.
Energy is violated: the total kinetic energy afterwards is 1.6 J, up from 0.4 J.
Both laws are violated, and the total kinetic energy afterwards is 2.4 J.
Neither law is violated, and the total kinetic energy afterwards is 0.4 J.
quiz.why: Momentum: before 0.2 × 2 = 0.4; after 0.2 × (-2) + 0.2 × 4 = 0.4, so momentum is fine. Energy: before ½ × 0.2 × 2² = 0.4 J; after ½ × 0.2 × 2² + ½ × 0.2 × 4² = 0.4 + 1.6 = 2.0 J, so energy would be created from nothing.
quiz.source: Momentum deck slides 8-9 (0.2 kg mass added for this site, outside source)

img.alt: A red ball moving left at 2 m/s and a black 8-ball moving right at 4 m/s.

quiz.q: Two carts collide on a nearly frictionless track and lock together. Which statement must be true if external forces are negligible?
options: The carts' total momentum after impact equals their total momentum before impact.
Each cart keeps its original velocity after the collision.
The carts' total kinetic energy must be unchanged.
The heavier cart must transfer all of its momentum to the lighter cart.
The system's momentum becomes zero because the carts stick together.
quiz.why: With negligible external force, the combined system's momentum is conserved. The carts can change velocity and lose kinetic energy in a sticking collision, but their total momentum remains the same.
quiz.source: Momentum deck: conservation of momentum; original ACEIT collision question

quiz.q: Why does a rifle kick backward when it fires a bullet?
options: Gravity pulls the rifle toward the shooter.
By conservation of momentum, the bullet's forward momentum is matched by the rifle's backward momentum.
The explosion creates new energy that pushes the rifle back.
Air in front of the barrel pushes back on the rifle.
Some of the gunpowder's mass is converted into energy (E = mc²).
quiz.why: Total momentum starts at zero and must stay zero, so the rifle gets backward momentum equal to the bullet's forward momentum.
quiz.source: Momentum deck slide 2; Practice questions Q14

quiz.q: A large spinning star collapses into a much smaller neutron star. What happens to its rotation?
options: It spins more slowly, because it has less surface area.
It spins at the same rate, because no outside force acted.
Its angular momentum increases, so it spins faster.
Its angular momentum decreases, but it spins faster.
It spins much faster, because its radius shrank while its angular momentum stayed the same.
quiz.why: No outside torque means L = mvr stays constant. A smaller r forces a larger v.
quiz.source: Momentum deck slide 12; Practice questions Q15

quiz.q: A cowboy is swinging a lasso and lets out more rope. Which of the following will happen due to conservation of angular momentum?
options: The rotation rate will slow down, since the radial distance to the loop end of the rope has increased.
The rotation rate will increase, since the speed of the loop end of the rope has increased.
The rotation rate will stay the same as long as the mass of the rope remains constant.
The rotation rate will slow down, since the loop end of the rope has to traverse a larger distance at the same speed.
The cowboy will start spinning.
quiz.why: L = mvr is constant, so a bigger r means a smaller v. The speed itself drops, so option D, which assumes the same speed, is wrong.
quiz.source: Momentum deck slide 12; Practice Test 2 Q12

quiz.q: Which has more thermal energy: a large pot of boiling water (100 °C) or a tiny firework spark (1000 °C)?
options: The pot of water, because it has vastly more particles, so its total kinetic energy is greater.
The spark, because it has a higher temperature.
They have equal thermal energy.
The spark, because it has more mass.
Neither, because only moving objects have thermal energy.
quiz.why: Thermal energy is total kinetic energy, so it depends on temperature and the amount of matter. Temperature is only the average per particle.
quiz.source: Energy deck slides 5-6; Practice questions Q18

quiz.q: Which of these statements is NOT correct?
options: Temperature is the average kinetic energy of the particles in a substance.
Thermal energy is the total kinetic energy of the particles in a substance.
Water boils at 373.15 K, which is 100 °C.
Absolute zero is 0 K, which is -273.15 °C.
Two objects at the same temperature always have the same thermal energy.
quiz.why: Thermal energy also depends on how much matter there is, so equal temperatures can mean very different thermal energies.
quiz.source: Energy deck slides 4-6

quiz.q:
Which statements about energy are correct?
I. Temperature and thermal energy measure exactly the same thing.
II. A rock perched on a ledge has gravitational potential energy because it could fall.
III. The random motion of the atoms in a parked car gives it more thermal energy than the car's kinetic energy at highway speed.
options: I only
I and II only
I and III only
II and III only
all of the above
quiz.why: I is false: temperature is the average per particle while thermal energy is the total. II is true. III is true: a car's thermal energy is about 1 × 10⁸ J while its kinetic energy at highway speed is about 1 × 10⁶ J.
quiz.source: Cosmic Perspective 4.3, Table 4.1 and 'Thermal Energy' (p.120); Energy deck slides 4-8

quiz.q: A ball is thrown straight up. At the very top of its flight (ignore air), compared with the moment it left the hand, the ball has
options: more gravitational potential energy and less kinetic energy.
more kinetic energy and less gravitational potential energy.
the same kinetic energy and more potential energy.
less of both kinds of energy, because energy is used up on the way up.
more of both kinds of energy.
quiz.why: Kinetic energy converts to potential energy on the way up. At the top the ball's speed is momentarily zero, so the kinetic energy is lowest and the stored energy is highest. The total is unchanged.
quiz.source: Energy deck slide 8; Cosmic Perspective Figure 4.15a

img.alt: A ball thrown in an arc from a hand, with more potential energy at the top and more kinetic energy near the ground.

quiz.q: Why does the center of a gas cloud get hot as the cloud shrinks under its own gravity?
options: Energy is created when gravity pulls on the gas.
Gravitational potential energy is converted into thermal energy.
The gas particles lose kinetic energy and heat up.
Mass is destroyed completely, leaving only heat.
Light from outside the cloud heats it.
quiz.why: The particles fall inward and lose potential energy. By conservation of energy that energy has to go somewhere, and it becomes the random motion of the particles, which is thermal energy.
quiz.source: Cosmic Perspective 4.3, Figure 4.15b; Energy deck slides 8-9

img.alt: A big gray gas cloud shrinking into a small hot glow, with labels for stored gravitational energy and thermal energy.

quiz.q: A satellite in low Earth orbit slowly loses altitude because of drag from the thin upper atmosphere. What happens to its orbital energy?
options: It increases, so the satellite moves to a higher orbit.
It stays exactly the same.
It decreases, turning into heat, so the satellite gradually falls toward Earth.
It is converted into extra mass for the satellite.
It is transferred to the Moon.
quiz.why: Energy cannot vanish. The satellite's orbital energy goes into thermal energy of the air, so the satellite has less and drops.
quiz.source: Energy deck slides 2, 9; Practice questions Q19; textbook 4.5 Atmospheric Drag

quiz.q: Which combination of base units is equivalent to the joule, the unit of energy?
options: kg × m/s²
kg × m/s
kg × m²/s
kg × m²/s²
m/s²
quiz.why: 1 J = 1 N × m = 1 kg × m²/s². The newton (kg × m/s²) is force, kg × m/s is momentum, kg × m²/s is angular momentum and m/s² is acceleration.
quiz.source: Energy deck slide 1; Momentum deck slides 3 and 10

quiz.q: An adult needs about 2500 food Calories per day, and 1 Calorie is about 4184 J. A candy bar supplies about 1 × 10⁶ J. About how many candy bars equal one day of food energy?
quiz.why: 2500 × 4184 = 10,460,000 J, about 1 × 10⁷ J. Dividing by 1 × 10⁶ J per candy bar gives about 10 candy bars.
quiz.source: Cosmic Perspective 4.3, text before Table 4.1 (p.120)

quiz.q: In the picture, gasoline is shown as stored energy. A car burns it and drives down the road. Which energy change has happened?
options: Kinetic energy of the car turns into potential energy in the gasoline.
Radiative energy of sunlight turns into chemical energy inside the engine.
Potential energy is created from nothing while the engine runs.
The gasoline loses all of its mass, which becomes light.
Chemical potential energy in the gasoline turns into kinetic energy of the car (plus some thermal energy).
quiz.why: Gasoline holds chemical potential energy. Burning it releases that energy, which becomes the kinetic energy of the moving car and some thermal energy. Energy changes form but is never created.
quiz.source: Cosmic Perspective 4.3, Figure 4.11 (p.120)

img.alt: Three photos joined by arrows: racing cyclists for kinetic energy, sunlight on a sunflower for radiative energy and a gasoline pump for potential energy.

quiz.q: A 0.2 kg red ball moving right at 2 m/s hits an identical black ball at rest (as in the picture). Afterwards the red ball is still moving right, at 0.5 m/s. What is the black ball's speed, and what happens to the total kinetic energy?
options: 1.5 m/s; it stays at 0.40 J.
1.5 m/s; it falls from 0.40 J to 0.25 J.
2.5 m/s; it rises from 0.40 J to 0.65 J.
1.0 m/s; it falls from 0.40 J to 0.125 J.
2.0 m/s; it rises from 0.40 J to 0.425 J.
quiz.why: Momentum: 0.2 × 2 = 0.2 × 0.5 + 0.2 × v, so v = 1.5 m/s. Kinetic energy: before ½ × 0.2 × 2² = 0.40 J; after ½ × 0.2 × 0.5² + ½ × 0.2 × 1.5² = 0.025 + 0.225 = 0.25 J. The 0.15 J lost became heat and sound.
quiz.source: Cosmic Perspective 4.3, Figure 4.8 (pool balls; numbers made for this site, outside source); Momentum deck slides 4-9

img.alt: A red ball moving right toward a black 8-ball at rest, labeled red: 2 m/s right and black: at rest.

quiz.q: Use c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s. How much mass must be completely converted into energy to release 4.5 × 10¹⁶ J?
options: 0.5 kg
5 kg
2 kg
quiz.why: m = E / c² = 4.5 × 10¹⁶ / (9 × 10¹⁶) = 0.5 kg. Using c instead of c² gives 1.5 × 10⁸ kg, and a 1 kg rock would give 9 × 10¹⁶ J, twice as much.
quiz.source: Energy deck slide 7; Cosmic Perspective Mathematical Insight 4.2

order.title: From the Big Bang to a thrown baseball
order.prompt: Put the steps in the order the energy travels, from the earliest source to the moving ball.
order.why: Hydrogen's mass-energy from the Big Bang is released by fusion in the Sun as sunlight. Plants turn sunlight into food, muscles release the food's chemical energy to move the arm, and the arm gives the ball its kinetic energy.

order.title: Temperature from coldest to hottest
order.prompt: Order these from the lowest temperature to the highest.
order.why: Absolute zero is 0 K, water freezes at 273.15 K and boils at 373.15 K, and oven air at about 200 °C (400 °F) is about 473 K.

order.title: Energy sizes from small to huge
order.prompt: Order these amounts of energy from the smallest to the largest.
order.why: In joules: sunlight on 1 m² for 1 s is about 1.3 × 10³, a candy bar 1 × 10⁶, a day of food 1 × 10⁷, 1 liter of oil 3.4 × 10⁷, fission of 1 kg of uranium-235 5.6 × 10¹³ and a 1-megaton H-bomb 4 × 10¹⁵.

layers.name: A day of food for an adult

order.title: Test a collision story
order.prompt: Put the steps for checking a proposed collision result in the order you would do them.
order.why: First find the total momentum before and after (with signs) and see if they match. Then work out the kinetic energy before and after, because energy can fall but must not rise.

layers.name: Add m × v of all balls before the hit
Add m × v of all balls after the hit
Check that the two momentum totals match
Find ½ m v² of all balls before and after
Check that the energy did not go up

sort.title: Which kind of energy?
sort.prompt: Sort each example into kinetic, potential or radiative energy.

items.text: A cyclist riding fast
A rock falling
A planet orbiting the Sun
Atoms jiggling inside a hot rock (thermal energy)
Gasoline in a car's tank
A rock perched on a ledge
Food that is not yet eaten
The mass of a rock (E = mc²)
A gas cloud spread out under its own gravity
Sunlight warming a planet's surface
Light that lets your eyes see
The glow of a light bulb

sort.why: Motion energy (including thermal energy) is kinetic, stored energy (chemical, gravitational, mass-energy) is potential, and energy carried by light is radiative.

sort.title: Which law explains it?
sort.prompt: Sort each situation by the conservation law that explains it best.

items.text: A rifle kicks backward when it fires
A rocket speeds forward as gas shoots out the back
A spacecraft coasts with its engines off
One pool ball hands its motion to another
Earth moves faster when closer to the Sun
A skater spins faster when she pulls in her arms
A collapsing star spins faster
A lasso slows when more rope is let out
A ball slows rising and speeds up falling
A shrinking gas cloud gets hot
Fusion turns some mass into light
Drag heats the air and a satellite sinks

sort.why: Straight-line motion and recoil come from momentum, spinning and orbiting from angular momentum, and trades between forms (motion, height, heat, light, mass) from energy.

sort.title: Is this collision possible?
sort.prompt: A red ball at 2 m/s hits an identical black ball at rest. Sort each proposed result by whether it obeys both laws (momentum and no energy gain).

items.text: Red stops; black moves right at 2 m/s
They stick together and move right at 1 m/s
Red 0.5 m/s right; black 1.5 m/s right
Red 0.25 m/s right; black 1.75 m/s right
Red bounces back at 2 m/s; black stays at rest
Red bounces back at 2 m/s; black moves right at 4 m/s
Red bounces back at 1 m/s; black moves right at 3 m/s
Red stops; black moves right at 1 m/s
Both balls move right at 2 m/s
Red moves left at 1 m/s; black moves right at 1 m/s

sort.why: With equal masses m the starting momentum is 2m and the starting kinetic energy is 2m. Allowed results keep the momentum at 2m and have kinetic energy of at most 2m. Failing the first check breaks momentum, and passing it with more than 2m of energy breaks energy conservation.
